items.notes: Valid fixes include: change the line-104 condition to check the Grafana prom rule (e.g. `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(promRule)`) and build/supply a `RulerGrafanaRuleDTO`-shaped object such as `{ grafana_alert: { uid: promRule.uid } }` when `rule` is absent; or change `SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer` to accept a uid / the prom rule. A fix that merely gates the Silence menu item out when `rule` is undefined would stop the no-op but removes silence from the list view, which the added `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` wiring implies is intended to work, so prefer actually opening the drawer. Only the Grafana-alerting case should open this drawer; recording/datasource rules must not. Note the V1 `RulesTable/RuleActionsButtons.tsx` uses the same `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule.rulerRule)` guard but always has a ruler rule, so it is not affected.

items.defectStatement: In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, when it is called with `rule === undefined` (which `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`/`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` pass when they receive `skipToken`), `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` returns `loading: false`, so `MaybeSupported` becomes `AlwaysSupported` and `duplicateSupported` stays supported (`isPluginProvidedRule(undefined)` is false). The Duplicate ability therefore becomes `[true, hasPermission('grafana' rules create)]`. `AlertRuleMenu` ORs this into `canDuplicate` (line 91-92) alongside the ruler ability, so for every non-Grafana / data-source rule the Duplicate menu item is enabled whenever the user can create Grafana-managed rules, even when the ruler ability says duplication is not supported.
obligations: When `rule` is undefined (skipToken path through useGrafanaPromRuleAbility/useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities), the Duplicate ability's supported flag must be false so it can never satisfy the OR in AlertRuleMenu.
With `rule` undefined, no returned ability should report `supported === true` merely because nothing is loading (i.e. the skipToken case must not fall through to AlwaysSupported).

For a defined, non-loading GrafanaPromRuleDTO, existing behavior must be preserved: Duplicate supported except for plugin-provided rules; Update/Delete/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently gated by immutability; silence/export gated by their rule-type flags.
While `loading` is true (folder/ruler info still resolving) abilities must remain unsupported, as before.
items.notes: The finding is accurate and the root cause is that Duplicate is the only AlertRuleMenu-consumed ability whose `allowed` flag uses a global Grafana permission (`rulesPermissions.create`) rather than a rule-specific value, so it is the only one that can become `[true, true]` in the skipToken case (Update/Delete get `[true, false]` and cannot be ORed on). Fixing the hook's supported flag is valid; alternatively the OR in AlertRuleMenu.tsx could be made source-aware, but the finding asks for the hook. Caveat: the suggested one-liner (`!rule || loading ? NotSupported : AlwaysSupported`) only changes `MaybeSupported`, so `View` and `Explore` (which use `AlwaysSupported` directly) will still return `[true, ...]` for undefined rules; the finding's "return NotSupported for every ability" is therefore slightly broader than its own example, though View/Explore are not ORed into any menu item, so they are not the source of the observed bug.

items.defectStatement: In GrafanaRuleListItem the actions element passes only `promRule={rule}` to RuleActionsButtons.V2, so AlertRuleMenu receives `rulerRule === undefined`. AlertRuleMenu gates the pause control with `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) && groupIdentifier.groupOrigin === 'grafana'`, which is false when no ruler rule is supplied. Even though the prom-rule pause ability (useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities) correctly reports supported+allowed for an editable Grafana alerting rule, MenuItemPauseRule never renders, so Grafana rules in the new list lose their Pause/Resume action.
obligations: For a Grafana-managed alerting rule rendered through GrafanaRuleListItem (only promRule available), the Pause/Resume menu item must render whenever the prom-rule pause ability is supported and allowed (i.e. canPause is true).

The rendered Pause/Resume item must use the prom rule's own state and uid: it shows 'Resume evaluation' when the rule is paused (isPaused / grafana_alert.is_paused) and 'Pause evaluation' otherwise, and invoking it pauses/unpauses that same rule via usePauseRuleInGroup(groupIdentifier, <rule uid>, newIsPaused).
Pause must still be suppressed for non-applicable rules: non-Grafana sources, recording rules, provisioned/immutable rules, and when groupIdentifier.groupOrigin is not 'grafana'.

Existing callers that pass an actual rulerRule (StateView, DataSourceGroupLoader, DataSourceRuleLoader, and other AlertRuleMenu consumers) must keep working unchanged, including the ruler-rule pause path and the surrounding menu items/dividers.
items.notes: The finding is accurate: with only promRule passed, the `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` gate is the blocker, not the ability calculation. Valid fixes include extending MenuItemPauseRule/AlertRuleMenu to accept the prom rule (using its uid + isPaused) or supplying/fetching the corresponding ruler rule; several implementations are acceptable as long as the pause ability decision and the actual API call use the correct rule. Trap: MenuItemPauseRule currently consumes RulerGrafanaRuleDTO (grafana_alert.uid, grafana_alert.is_paused, isPausedRule), so adapting it to GrafanaPromRuleDTO requires mapping uid/isPaused. Out-of-scope but related: the Delete menu item in AlertRuleMenu is also gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`, so a caller passing only promRule likewise loses Delete; the cited finding only concerns pause.

items.defectStatement: The cleanup loop's ticker interval was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute (cleanup.go:77), so `srv.clean(ctx)` — which runs all eight cleanup jobs (tmp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) — now fires ~10x more often, multiplying DB/IO load with no accompanying justification or config gating. The `const timeout = 9 * time.Minute` in `clean` indicates the loop was designed around a ~10-minute cadence, reinforcing that 1 minute is a regression.
obligations: The periodic cleanup cadence must not run every cleanup job once per minute; restore the previous interval (10 minutes) or otherwise ensure the full job set is not invoked 10x more frequently than before.

If a faster cadence is genuinely needed, it must be scoped/gated (e.g. a separate annotation-only schedule or an explicit config value with a sensible default) rather than speeding up the single global ticker.
Preserve existing behavior: `srv.cleanUpTmpFiles(ctx)` still runs once synchronously at startup before the loop, and the loop still returns ctx.Err() when ctx is done.
Do not introduce overlapping/concurrent execution of the cleanup jobs (the current synchronous single-goroutine loop must stay serialized).
items.notes: The performance claim is valid; note the loop calls clean synchronously in one goroutine, so runs do not overlap — the harm is frequency/load, not concurrency. Because ticker.C has capacity 1, ticks are dropped while a run exceeds 1 minute, but the effect is still near-continuous full-set cleanup versus the prior 10-minute spacing. Legitimate alternative fixes: revert to `time.Minute * 10`; or add a configurable interval (the repo has no cleanup-interval setting today — only `cleanupjob_batchsize` in conf/defaults.ini). The finding's "annotation-only job/config" suggestion is an acceptable gating option but not the only valid one.

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Delete's success path, recordStorageDuration is called with `name` (the deleted object's name) as the third argument, but that argument populates the Prometheus `kind` label (see metrics.go: `[]string{"is_error","mode","kind","method"}`). The success sample is therefore mislabeled with an object name instead of `options.Kind`, and it creates one series per object name, causing unbounded label cardinality; it is also inconsistent with the error branch (line 103) and the other methods, which pass `options.Kind`.
obligations: The successful Delete storage-duration recording must pass options.Kind as the kind-label value (same as the error branch at line 103 and the other Mode3 methods).
The call must remain recordStorageDuration (storage metric), with isError=false, mode3Str, method "delete", and startStorage unchanged.
No other behavior of Delete may change: it still returns (res, async, err) and still launches the async legacy delete goroutine with options.Kind for the legacy metric.
items.notes: Only the cited line changes: `name` -> `options.Kind`. Note the helper signature names that parameter `name` (metrics.go:59), which may mislead; the underlying HistogramVec label is `kind`. Unrelated defects exist in the same file (Update error path uses recordLegacyDuration at line 129; DeleteCollection legacy goroutine uses recordStorageDuration at line 166) and should NOT be changed by a fix for this finding. The finding's claim is accurate.

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Create the asynchronous legacy write's result is only converted to a metric label: `_, errObjectSt := d.Legacy.Create(...)` followed by `d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, ...)`, so when the legacy write fails (e.g. times out after the 10s context cause or errors for any other reason) the error is never logged. Pre-PR code did log legacy create failures, and drift between legacy and unified storage is now invisible in logs.
obligations: When errObjectSt is non-nil in the async legacy Create goroutine, emit an error-level log that includes the error value (using the context/goroutine logger, e.g. log or klog.FromContext(ctx)); when it is nil, no error log is emitted.
Preserve the metric call d.recordLegacyDuration(errObjectSt != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) so the legacy-duration/error metric behavior is unchanged.

Preserve the async semantics: Create must still return the Storage result and error to the caller regardless of the legacy outcome, and the legacy write must still run in a goroutine with the 10s timeout and its context cancellation.
Do not change the caller-visible return values or the fact that legacy failures are not propagated to the caller.
items.notes: The same dropped-error pattern exists in the other async legacy goroutines of this file (Delete line ~113, Update line ~140, DeleteCollection line ~166); a thorough fix may log there too, but the cited lines are only Create 55-56. A valid fix could also inline the log inside the metric branch; a defensible alternative is logging unconditionally with a nil-guard. Note line 166 records recordStorageDuration for the legacy DeleteCollection call (likely a separate bug) and line 45/106 use mismatched args (startStorage/name) — out of scope for this finding.

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Update the asynchronous legacy write at line 139 passes the original objInfo to d.Legacy.Update instead of a wrapper carrying the object already committed to unified storage. Legacy storage therefore re-invokes the original UpdatedObjectInfo (recomputing the patch/merge) against its own old object, which can be stale or differ from the unified-store old object, producing a different result or a failed legacy write even though the unified write succeeded. This regresses the pre-change behavior, which handed legacy an updateWrapper whose updated object was the one returned by Storage.Update.
obligations: The UpdatedObjectInfo passed to d.Legacy.Update must yield the exact object returned by d.Storage.Update (the value bound to res), not re-evaluate the caller's original info against the legacy store's own old object.
Preconditions() on the info given to the legacy update must still delegate to the original objInfo's Preconditions (so resourceVersion/UID precondition checks continue to apply).

All other arguments to d.Legacy.Update (name, createValidation, updateValidation, forceAllowCreate, options) and the surrounding async/10s-timeout/metric behavior must be preserved; the return value still is res, async, err from the unified store.
The create-on-update path (forceAllowCreate with no existing object) must still cause the legacy store to end up with the same committed object as unified storage.
items.notes: The finding is accurate. res is the runtime.Object returned by Storage.Update, so wrapping with &updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res} (the updateWrapper lives in dualwriter.go and returns u.updated unconditionally while delegating Preconditions) is the canonical fix, matching pre-change mode3 and current mode2 usage. Alternative valid fixes exist (e.g. call objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, res) and pass that result via a wrapper), so grading should check the behavior, not one specific construction. Note the error from the legacy update is only recorded via recordLegacyDuration and intentionally not propagated (async side effect); a fix must not change that. Also note this legacy call runs in a goroutine using a timeout-bound ctx, so a fix should not introduce a fresh legacy read/UpdatedObject round-trip that defeats the wrapper intent.

items.defectStatement: In DualWriterMode3.Delete (pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:99-105), any error from d.Storage.Delete now triggers an early return, so when Storage returns a NotFound (an object that exists only in the legacy store or was already removed from Storage) the legacy delete is never attempted. The previous implementation (shown in the diff) only returned early for non-NotFound errors and still ran d.Legacy.Delete on IsNotFound, so this change leaves orphaned legacy copies and breaks the write-to-both-stores invariant.
obligations: When d.Storage.Delete returns an error for which apierrors.IsNotFound(err) is true, the method must NOT return early; it must still attempt the legacy delete (d.Legacy.Delete with the same name, deleteValidation and options), so a legacy-only object is cleaned up.
When d.Storage.Delete returns a non-NotFound error, the method must still return early and must not call d.Legacy.Delete (preserve the existing fail-fast behavior for real errors).
The success path must be preserved: when Storage.Delete succeeds, the legacy delete is still attempted (with its existing timeout/goroutine handling) and the returned result/values are unchanged.

Observable return/metrics contracts are preserved: the storage error still propagates to the caller on the NotFound path (as before, the caller receives the storage NotFound error, not a silent success), and recordStorageDuration(true, ...) is still invoked when Storage.Delete errors.
items.notes: The cited lines remove the apierrors import; a fix restoring tolerance must re-add `apierrors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"` (the added `errors` import is for the timeout cause). Multiple implementations are valid (e.g. `if err != nil && !apierrors.IsNotFound(err) { ... return }`, or an inner `if apierrors.IsNotFound(err)` branch), as long as legacy delete still runs on NotFound and return values match the pre-change behavior. Out of scope but visible in the same hunk: line 106 passes `name` instead of `options.Kind` to recordStorageDuration, and line 97 sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` instead of `log`; do not treat those as part of this finding. Msg is not required to re-add the old `deleted, async, err` logging; only the control flow matters.

items.defectStatement: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/terminate() call self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the FixedQueuePool is created once by ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py:133) and reused for every create_with_partitions call, so a rebalance/partition reassignment that closes the old strategy permanently shuts down the shared worker threads and queues; the next strategy's submits then hit a shut-down pool (queue.put raises ShutDown, offsets leak). Separately, each create_with_partitions spawns a fresh commit_thread sharing one OffsetTracker, and terminate() sets shutdown_event but never joins that thread, so a stale commit loop/callback can keep running.
obligations: close() and terminate() must not shut down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool: the pool must remain usable for strategies returned by later create_with_partitions calls (rebalances). Teardown of the pool stays the responsibility of the factory (ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown()).

close() and terminate() must stop and join this strategy's own commit_thread so no stale commit loop keeps calling its commit_function against the shared OffsetTracker after the strategy is closed/terminated.
terminate() must actually halt its commit thread (it currently only sets shutdown_event without joining), not just leave it running.
Preserve existing behavior: shutdown_event still prevents further commits, commit_function is still invoked with get_committable_offsets() results, and join() still delegates to close().
items.notes: Primary defect is the queue_pool.shutdown() call in the strategy lifecycle — the fix is to remove it from close()/terminate() (optionally leaving pool shutdown only in factory.shutdown()). Any equivalent that keeps the shared pool alive across strategy instances is acceptable. The missing join in terminate() is a secondary point; a fix may join with a timeout or otherwise guarantee the thread terminates. Note factory.shutdown() already shuts down the pool and sets self.queue_pool = None, and the test tearDown calls close() so the pool must survive close().

items.defectStatement: In FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue_consumer.py:184-185) each work queue is created as queue.Queue() with the default maxsize=0, i.e. unbounded, and submit() (lines 204-212) enqueues with a bare put() and no depth check. When producers outpace the single worker per queue, items accumulate without limit and a traffic burst can exhaust memory; the class docstring of SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy even claims "Natural backpressure when queues fill up", which does not exist here.
obligations: Each of the num_queues work queues must be given a finite capacity (maxsize > 0) instead of the current unbounded queue.Queue().

When a queue is full, submit() must apply backpressure to the caller (e.g. block until space is available) rather than silently discarding the work item, so no message is lost and no tracked offset is left permanently outstanding.

Existing public behavior must be preserved: FixedQueuePool(result_processor=..., identifier=..., num_queues=N) with no capacity argument still works (sensible default), and get_queue_for_group, get_stats(), wait_until_empty(), shutdown(), and FIFO ordering-per-group continue to function.

Offset-tracker semantics must stay consistent: any item that is actually enqueued must still get its offset recorded and eventually complete_offset()-ed by the worker; any path that refuses/drops an item must not leave its offset marked outstanding.
items.notes: The finding is accurate; queue.Queue() is unbounded. Preferred fix: add a maxsize parameter to FixedQueuePool (default e.g. a few thousand) and pass it to queue.Queue(maxsize=...), keeping submit()'s blocking put() so the arroyo consumer thread naturally throttles upstream. Note submit() currently calls offset_tracker.add_offset() BEFORE put(); a fix that switches to non-blocking put_nowait and drops on Full must also remove/complete that offset, otherwise offsets stall forever. The worker loop already uses queue.get() with queue.shutdown(immediate=False), so a bounded queue is safe with the existing shutdown path. Tests construct FixedQueuePool with only result_processor/identifier/num_queues, so the new capacity argument must be optional. Alternative valid fixes: explicit qsize() depth check/limit in submit(), or a semaphore — as long as overflow results in upstream backpressure and not silent data loss.

items.defectStatement: `_commit_loop` runs on a daemon background thread started in `__init__` and calls `self.commit_function` directly. `commit_function` is the Arroyo `Commit` callback (see `result_consumer.py:249-252`), which mutates stream-processor/consumer commit state and is by design driven from the processor's main thread (the `submit`/`poll` loop). Invoking it concurrently from this thread races with `poll`/Arroyo's `_run_once`, and because the strategy has no awareness of partition revocation it can also commit tracked offsets after those partitions have been reassigned. Additionally `terminate()` never stops/joins the commit thread, so commits can be issued after shutdown.
obligations: `self.commit_function` must not be invoked concurrently with the processor's main-thread methods (`submit`/`poll`/`close`/`terminate`); commits must be either performed on the main thread or serialized by a shared lock so they cannot race with `poll`/`_run_once` and consumer state mutation.

Only offsets that are actually committable and safe (highest contiguous fully-processed offset per partition) may be passed to `commit_function`; the +1 convention applied in `result_consumer.commit_offsets` must be preserved, and no not-yet-processed/outstanding offset may be committed.

`offset_tracker.mark_committed(partition, offset)` must be called for exactly the offsets handed to `commit_function`, and only after the commit succeeds; the `offsets_committed` metric must still be emitted for committed offsets.

After `close()`/`terminate()`, no further `commit_function` calls may occur (pending committable offsets are dropped) and the commit thread must be stopped/joined, without breaking graceful shutdown of the queue pool.
items.notes: Valid alternative fixes: (a) remove the background thread and compute/hand off committable offsets so `commit_function` is called from `poll()`, or (b) keep the thread but guard both the thread's commit path and the main-thread commit path with a lock and drop commits once shutdown/closed. A grader should accept either. Preserve existing observable behavior tested in test_queue_consumer.py (`test_offset_committing` expects commit to eventually happen with timeout, e.g. committed offset 104 for offsets 100-104) so a fail-closed thread that never commits, or one that commits only on close, would regress. The finding's "commit for revoked partitions" claim is plausible but secondary: the strategy tracks only offsets it has seen and has no rebalance callback, so the concrete, verifiable defect is the cross-thread invocation of the Arroyo commit callback (and the missing join in `terminate`), not a demonstrated commit of a revoked partition. Note the original also leaves a window between `get_committable_offsets` and `mark_committed`; if `commit_function` raises, `mark_committed` is skipped, which is acceptable (offsets get retried) and need not be changed.

items.defectStatement: In test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling the final assertion (line 1922) claims that a processing failure leaves the partition uncommitted, but the implementation contradicts this: OrderedQueueWorker.run calls offset_tracker.complete_offset in its finally block (queue_consumer.py:148-149) even when result_processor raises, so both offsets (100 failed, 101 succeeded) are marked complete, OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets returns 101, and the strategy's commit loop adds +1 (result_consumer.py:249-252) and commits 102. The assertion only holds because the test checks before the commit thread's ~1-second tick fires, making it timing-dependent and asserting the opposite of the real behavior.
obligations: The test must assert that after both messages are processed (processor raises for 100, succeeds for 101) the test partition IS committed with value 102 (the next offset to read), i.e. a failure in one message does not prevent progress/commit for the batch, replacing the 'not in committed_offsets' assertion with a check that the partition is present and equals 102.

The test must wait deterministically for the commit (poll track_commits/committed_offsets until the partition appears, with a bounded timeout longer than the ~1s commit loop interval) instead of relying on a fixed 0.2s sleep, so the assert cannot race the commit thread.

Preserve the existing error-handling intent and setup: both messages are still submitted, mock_processor_call.call_count == 2 is still asserted, and the docstring intent (errors don't block offset commits for other messages) is retained.
The test must remain non-flaky regardless of commit-thread timing: it should not assert absence of a commit for the partition under any fixed timing window.
items.notes: Finding is accurate as written. Key numbers: commit_function adds +1 (result_consumer.py:249-252), so a processed offset of 101 yields committed 102; be careful not to assert 101. The commit loop ticks at 1.0s intervals (queue_consumer.py:273-289), so the deterministic wait needs to exceed ~1s. Note that ResultProcessor.__call__ normally swallows exceptions (result_consumer.py:44-54); the test patches type(...).__call__ with side_effect so the exception escapes to the worker, which is exactly the path that still completes the offset in finally. Alternative valid fix (different location): change production code so a failed processing does not call complete_offset, in which case the original no-commit assertion would become correct — but for a fix confined to the cited test lines, asserting a committed offset of 102 is the right behavior. Do not accept a fix that merely reorders/shortens the sleep or weakens the assertion to something like 'eventually not committed'.

items.defectStatement: In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset) unconditionally, so when result_processor raises the failed message's offset is marked complete. The commit loop (SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop via get_committable_offsets) then sees the offset as processed and commits it (and offset+1), which contradicts the documented guarantee "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and silently drops the failed message.
obligations: When result_processor completes without raising, complete_offset(partition, offset) must still be invoked so the work item becomes committable (success-path behavior preserved).

When result_processor raises a non-ShutDown Exception, complete_offset must NOT be invoked for that work item, so the offset stays in outstanding and get_committable_offsets will not advance the committed offset past it.

The queue-depth metrics gauge (remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth) and the exception logging must still be emitted on both success and failure paths, and the queue.ShutDown handling must remain intact.
No regression to normal operation: FixedQueuePool / SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy runs where processing succeeds still produce the same committable offsets and commits as before.
items.notes: Valid finding; the shown code matches the finding. No existing test covers a raising result_processor (test_queue_consumer.py only exercises success paths and OffsetTracker directly), so a fix may need to rely on the behavioral requirement rather than existing tests. Multiple fixes are acceptable: a success flag set inside the try and checked before complete_offset in the finally, or moving complete_offset out of the finally to after the successful result_processor call (keeping the metrics gauge in the finally). Trap: the inner `except queue.ShutDown: break` also falls through the finally, so any success-flag approach must ensure the ShutDown branch does not complete the offset unintentionally; the core requirement is the generic Exception case. Note the offset is registered via add_offset in FixedQueuePool.submit before queuing, so leaving it outstanding is what blocks commits. Leaving it outstanding permanently stalls commits for that partition (there is no retry path), which is the intended 'block commits on error' behavior, not data loss.

items.defectStatement: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the decoder is called on `message.payload` before any inspection of `message.value`, but the decoder used in production (`ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload`, via `partial(self.decode_payload, self.topic_for_codec)`) starts with `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`. So a filtered message raises AssertionError, and because the recovery code in the `except` block runs `add_offset`/`complete_offset` only when `isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)`, a filtered message whose `message.value` is not a `BrokerValue` (e.g. `Message(Value(FILTERED_PAYLOAD, offsets))` as built in `src/sentry/consumers/dlq.py`) gets no offset tracking at all: the offset tracker never advances past it, commits stall and the offset is reprocessed, and every normal filter is logged as an error. (Note: when the filtered payload is wrapped in a `BrokerValue`, as in the existing test, the `except` block already records the offset, so the "skipped" claim does not apply to that representation.)
obligations: `submit` must not pass a `FilteredPayload` payload to `self.decoder` (the production decoder asserts `not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`), and must not treat a filtered message as a decoder failure (no spurious `logger.exception` / error path for ordinary filtered messages).

Filtered messages must have their offsets tracked so they cannot block commits: when the filtered message exposes partition/offset (value is `BrokerValue`) call `add_offset` then `complete_offset`; when it only exposes a committable mapping, record those offsets. A subsequent valid message on the same partition must be committable past the filtered offset (per `test_handles_invalid_messages`).

Existing behavior for normal `KafkaPayload` messages must be preserved: decode, `result is None` -> add_offset + complete_offset and return; non-None -> compute `grouping_fn` and `queue_pool.submit`; decoder/grouping exceptions still record the offset as complete so they neither block later commits nor loop.
`partition`/`offset` may only be read from a `BrokerValue`; the fix must not raise for either representation of a filtered message.
items.notes: The finding's mechanism is right for filtered messages whose `message.value` is not a `BrokerValue`, but overstated for the test's representation: `BrokerValue(FilteredPayload(), partition, offset, ...)` has `message.value` as a `BrokerValue`, so the current `except` block already adds+completes that offset and no reprocessing occurs there. Two real gaps remain: (1) plain filtered values (e.g. `Message(Value(FILTERED_PAYLOAD, offsets))` from dlq.py) get no tracking, and (2) every filtered message produces an AssertionError logged via `logger.exception`. `result_consumer.decode_payload`'s assert sits outside its try/except, so the AssertionError propagates to `submit`. Valid fixes include checking `isinstance(message.payload, FilteredPayload)` (or `message.value`) up front and recording offsets directly, or recording `message.committable` for filtered messages instead of relying on `BrokerValue`; the grader should accept either. The commit thread flushes `get_committable_offsets()` once per second, so correctness is about the tracker state, not the commit timing.

items.defectStatement: The finding overstates the impact. The cited loop does stop at the first offset that is missing from `all_offsets` (e.g. a never-delivered offset), so within a single `get_committable_offsets()` call it can return an offset below the real highest-safe offset when a gap exists. But it does NOT cause a permanent stall: `mark_committed()` (line 105) prunes every offset <= the committed offset from `all_offsets`, and `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` (lines 83-86) is recomputed each call, so `min_offset` moves past the gap on the next cycle and `start` begins above it. With offsets 100, 102, 103 (gap at 101) all complete, the first call commits 100, the next call commits 103. Worst case is one extra commit-loop interval (~1s) of delay across a gap, not "never commits again / lag grows forever".
obligations: Safety: must never report an offset that is greater than or equal to any offset that was passed to add_offset() but has not yet been passed to complete_offset(); committing past an outstanding delivered offset risks losing messages. (The existing code guarantees this by breaking on the first offset that is outstanding.)

Progress across gaps: once the highest completed offset below a never-delivered gap has been committed, offsets above that gap must become committable (at least on subsequent calls) so the partition does not stall — no gap may block commits indefinitely.

Preserve existing return semantics: return {} when no offset is newly committable; return the highest fully-committable offset per partition, across multiple partitions independently (test_simple_tracking and test_multiple_partitions must still hold).
Preserve the concurrency/state contract: per-partition locking, monotonic last_committed, and mark_committed pruning of committed offsets must keep working.
items.notes: The finding's mechanism (loop requires numerically contiguous offsets present in all_offsets) is accurately described, but its stated consequence is wrong; the min_offset/pruning interaction already recovers across gaps, so a behavior-preserving change (or no change) is a valid fix. A valid alternative fix if one wants to commit above a gap in the same cycle is to scan sorted(all_offsets) (or an ordered structure) from last_committed and commit up to the last offset with no outstanding delivered offset at or below it — but do NOT simply drop the `offset in all_offsets` check while still committing to max, since that could skip an outstanding delivered offset. Trap: the existing test `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` (tests/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/test_queue_consumer.py:351) asserts that a first batch of 100,102,103 commits only 100 until 101 arrives, i.e. it encodes gap-blocking; any fix that commits above a never-delivered gap immediately will contradict that assertion unless the test is updated. Also note offsets are delivered in ascending order per partition, so an "out-of-order" arrival of 101 after 102/103 (as that test submits) does not occur in real Kafka.

items.defectStatement: In SpanFlusher.join(), the `for` loop over self.processes breaks out as soon as the join deadline has elapsed (remaining_time <= 0), so the remaining multiprocessing processes are neither waited on nor terminate()d. Only the process being examined when the deadline passes is terminated; all later processes are skipped (or, if next_step.join already consumed the timeout, all of them are skipped). The previous single-process implementation always called terminate() after waiting, so a hung process past the deadline is no longer killed and is left to be reaped at interpreter exit.
obligations: After the join deadline elapses, every process remaining in self.processes must still be terminated (for multiprocessing.Process instances), not skipped; removing the `break` or terminating the leftover processes after the wait loop both satisfy this.

No process may be waited on past the deadline: the loop must stop sleeping/polling is_alive() once deadline has passed (the inner while condition `deadline is None or deadline > time.time()` must keep bounding the wait).
With timeout is None, behavior is preserved: wait until each process is no longer alive and then terminate multiprocessing.Process instances.
Only multiprocessing.Process instances are killed; threads created when produce_to_pipe is set must not have terminate() called on them and must not raise.
items.notes: The hung process itself is still terminated after its inner while exits; the defect is the processes after it (the finding's phrasing is accurate). A valid alternative fix is to keep the break for the waiting phase but add a separate pass that terminates all remaining (and un-terminated) processes. Note the deadline can also be exhausted by self.next_step.join(timeout) before the first process is looked at, so a correct fix should still terminate all processes even then. Tests use produce_to_pipe, which makes the entries threading.Thread, so terminate() must remain guarded by isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process).

items.defectStatement: In `WidgetCardChart.tableResultComponent` (static/app/views/dashboards/widgetCard/chart.tsx), when the `use-table-widget-visualization` flag is on, the new branch renders `TableWidgetVisualization` with hard-coded `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`, so every table widget shows an empty table even though the real `result.data`/`result.meta` and `widget.queries[i]` fields are available. Because `columns={[]}` is not nullish, it also bypasses `TableWidgetVisualization`'s `columns ?? fallback-from-meta.fields` logic, guaranteeing zero columns.
obligations: When the feature flag is enabled, the rendered TableWidgetVisualization must receive the current result's real rows and metadata (result.data plus result.meta's fields/units), not empty arrays/objects.

Must not pass an empty `columns` array; either omit the `columns` prop so TableWidgetVisualization derives columns from tableData.meta.fields, or pass populated TabularColumn entries derived from widget.queries[i] (field names via fieldAliases, type from result.meta).
The non-flag path (StyledSimpleTableChart with its eventView/fields/fieldAliases/metadata/data/loading props) must remain behaviorally unchanged.
The mapping over tableResults, per-result keying, and the existing undefined-tableResults loading placeholder must be preserved.
items.notes: The most direct valid fix is `tableData={{data: result.data, meta: result.meta}}` and dropping `columns` entirely, since TableWidgetVisualization falls back to meta.fields for column order (stories confirm columns is optional). A fix that additionally builds columns from `widget.queries[i].fields`/`fieldAliases` is also valid; grader should accept either. Note the finding's claim 'ignoring widget.queries[i]' is only relevant to the optional columns prop — data correctness comes from result, so omitting columns still fixes the data loss.

items.defectStatement: In useTraceItemAttributeKeys the React Query cache key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, and `queryOptions` is built only from traceItemType, type, datetime and project ids. The queryFn closes over `getTraceItemAttributeKeys`, which reads `organization.slug` to build the request URL, so the org is not represented in the key. Before this refactor the old `useApiQuery([path, endpointOptions])` key included `/organizations/${organization.slug}/...`. As a result, switching organizations while datetime/projects/type stay the same reuses the previous org's cached TagCollection and shows the wrong org's attribute keys until a refetch.
obligations: The query key must incorporate an organization identifier that changes when the active organization changes (e.g. organization.slug or organization.id), so two organizations with identical datetime/projects/type do not share cache.

All existing key inputs that affect the response must remain part of the key: traceItemType/itemType, attribute type, the datetime params (start/end/statsPeriod/utc) and the resolved project ids — changing any of these must still produce a different key.

The fetcher must keep requesting the correct organization's `/organizations/<org slug>/trace-items/attributes/` endpoint and returning the same TagCollection shape and error behavior; the returned `{attributes, error, isLoading}` API and the isFetching/previous fallback must be preserved.

The key must remain stable across re-renders when its inputs are unchanged (the organization identifier must be included where it is actually read/memoized), so the hook does not refetch on every render.
items.notes: Valid regression introduced by the refactor (Diff removed the org-bearing path from the key). Several fixes are acceptable: add organization.slug (or id) into the queryKey array in useTraceItemAttributeKeys, or fold it into makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions so it flows into queryOptions. Using organization.id is as valid as slug. Do not require adding environment to the key/options: useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys intentionally omits environment ("environment left out intentionally as it's not supported"). Also, `projectIds` is a fresh array each render when the `projects` prop is passed, but react-query hashes keys structurally, so that identity churn alone does not cause refetch and should not be treated as a defect here. Tests in useTraceItemAttributeKeys.spec.tsx render a single org and won't by themselves catch the cross-org bug.

items.defectStatement: In gen_request_data, error event timestamps are compared against rrweb replay event timestamps without unit conversion: error_events[error_idx]["timestamp"] comes from nodestore event data, which is in seconds (sentry/eventstore/models.py uses datetime.fromtimestamp), whereas rrweb replay event "timestamp" values are in milliseconds (e.g. 1674291701348). Because seconds-valued error timestamps are ~1000x smaller than millisecond event timestamps, every error compares as earlier than every event and is emitted before the first breadcrumb, so the chronological log order sent to Seer is wrong.
obligations: Errors and replay/breadcrumb events must be interleaved in true chronological order: an error must be emitted before the first event whose (converted) timestamp is greater than the error's, and after all earlier events.

The seconds-vs-milliseconds unit mismatch must be resolved by normalizing both sides to the same unit before comparison (multiplying the error timestamp by 1000, or dividing the event timestamp by 1000, are both acceptable).

Existing behaviors must be preserved: error_events are still sorted ascending by timestamp before interleaving, and any errors remaining after all segments are still emitted at the end via the trailing while loop.
Error log messages produced by generate_error_log_message remain unchanged in content for a given ErrorEvent (a fix that normalizes for comparison should not corrupt the emitted error message).
items.notes: Verified units: nodestore event "timestamp" is seconds (Event.datetime uses datetime.fromtimestamp; tests store now.timestamp()), while rrweb replay event "timestamp" is milliseconds (test fixtures use 1674291701348; replays/testutils.py ms() = seconds*1000). The finding is correct and not overstated. Trap: existing tests mask the bug by using second-valued replay event timestamps in test_get_request_data (1.5, 2.0) and float(now.timestamp()) in test_get_with_error, so they would still pass with either unit; a grader should judge on the production-format comparison, not those fixtures. Alternative valid fixes: convert the error timestamp to ms in the comparison, or divide the event timestamp by 1000; converting once at fetch time is also valid but would change the timestamp printed in the error log message.

items.defectStatement: In add-buffer.lua the size cap `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` evicts members strictly by lowest `end_timestamp_precise` score, with no exemption for the segment/root span (the member whose `span_id == set_span_id`). Since spans are stored with `end_timestamp_precise` as the ZSET score (buffer.py:197-199) and the root's timestamp can be lower than its children (e.g. remote/`is_remote` segment spans, clock skew), a segment with >1000 spans can lose its root; `flush_segments` then marks no span `is_segment` and `done_flush_segments` ships a segment without its root/segment span.
obligations: When span_count > 1000, the segment/root span member (the payload whose span_id equals set_span_id) must never be removed by the size-based eviction.
Eviction must still bound the set: after it runs, at most 1000 members remain (i.e. the surplus of span_count - 1000 lowest-`end_timestamp_precise` non-root members are removed).

All existing behavior must be preserved: the returned array {redirect_depth, span_key, set_key, has_root_span}, the redirect-chain resolution loop, the zunionstore/link merging of span_key and parent_key, the expire calls, the has_root_span key logic, and no eviction when span_count <= 1000.
A fix must not error or re-insert a bogus member when the segment span is not yet present in the set (e.g. root not yet arrived), and the whole add must stay within the single atomic Lua script.
items.notes: The cited code and its premise are accurate: zpopmin does remove lowest-scored members and the script never checks the root. The eviction is a bound/edge case, not guaranteed to hit the root on every >1000-span segment. Implementation note for graders: the root member is a serialized JSON payload and is not directly addressable by span_id inside the script (ARGV carries only span_id/parent_span_id, and buffer.py zadds payloads before EVALSHA), so a valid fix may need to pass the root payload/score as an extra argument or otherwise locate it; any mechanism is acceptable. If the fix re-adds the root it must restore its original `end_timestamp_precise` score. The pre-existing mismatch between the hardcoded 1000 and Python's `max_segment_spans=1001` is out of scope.

items.defectStatement: In add-buffer.lua, the two ZUNIONSTORE calls (lines 47 and 53) merge span_key/parent_key into set_key without an AGGREGATE option, so Redis uses the default SUM. When the same span payload (same sorted-set member) exists in both the destination set_key and the merged span_key/parent_key — e.g. a redelivered or duplicated span — its score is added, so instead of the span's end_timestamp_precise it becomes roughly twice that value. Because eviction (lines 62-64) uses zpopmin to drop the lowest scores and keep only the 1000 newest, such an inflated score makes the duplicate look like the newest span and it survives eviction while a genuinely older span is dropped, breaking the "keep the newest 1000, evict oldest first" behavior.
obligations: Both zunionstore calls (line 47 for span_key and line 53 for parent_key) must specify an aggregate that is not SUM — AGGREGATE MAX (or equivalently MIN) — so a member present in both sets keeps a valid end-timestamp score instead of a summed one.
The merged set must still contain the union of members (no span payload lost), and members present only once must retain their original end_timestamp_precise score.

The zunionstore return value must continue to be used as span_count (number of unique members in the resulting set), so the span_count == 0 -> zcard fallback and the span_count > 1000 -> zpopmin eviction still work.

The surrounding behavior must be preserved: is_root_span / redirect resolution, the `unlink span_key` / `unlink parent_key` calls, the `expire` on set_key, and the returned {redirect_depth, span_key, set_key, has_root_span} tuple.
items.notes: The finding is accurate: ZUNIONSTORE's documented default aggregate is SUM, and the code sets no AGGREGATE. MAX and MIN are both valid because the same member (payload bytes) is written with the same end_timestamp_precise, so they yield the same score; the only requirement is to stop summing. Note the destination set_key is also a source operand, which Redis permits. Scope of impact: scores are used for eviction (zpopmin keeps largest = newest) and not for output ordering (flush uses zscan, which is not score-ordered); duplicate members are only produced by redelivery/duplication, so the impact is limited to those cases, but the fix is still correct. Existing span-buffer tests (tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py) do not assert SUM behavior, so they should remain green.

items.defectStatement: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the redirect-chase loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000 (`for i = 0, 1000`). This couples the redirect-traversal depth limit to the new 1000-span eviction cap added in the same PR, but the two are unrelated: eviction (the `zpopmin` at lines 62-64) only trims spans from the set zset, while the redirect hash retains every `span_id -> set_span_id` mapping until TTL expiry, so a valid parent chain can exceed 1000 hops. When the loop exhausts its bound without breaking, the incoming span is linked to an intermediate set (line 40) instead of the true root, silently splitting/corrupting the segment.
obligations: The loop must resolve redirect chains longer than 1000 hops (e.g. restore the prior 10000 bound or otherwise fully resolve the chain); the traversal-depth limit must not be tied to the 1000-span eviction cap.
Eviction must remain unchanged: after merging, when the set exceeds 1000 spans, `zpopmin` still trims it to 1000 (lines 62-64).

Traversal semantics must be preserved: keep chasing via `hget(main_redirect_key, set_span_id)`, break when the value is nil (no redirect) or equals the current `set_span_id` (self/cycle), else set `set_span_id` to the returned value.

`redirect_depth` must still be assigned the number of hops actually followed and returned in the existing tuple `{redirect_depth, span_key, set_key, has_root_span}`, keeping the downstream min/max_redirect_depth metrics in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py` working.
items.notes: Finding is valid in substance. The only overstatement is "no functional need": the 1000 bound likely aimed to match the new 1000-span cap, but that is wrong because redirect mappings for evicted spans persist, so chain length is not bounded by current set size. A minimal valid fix restores the 10000 bound (optionally with the original explanatory comment); any fix that fully resolves the chain and leaves eviction untouched is acceptable. Note `for i = 0, 1000` already executes 1001 iterations; a correct fix should not alter the nil/self break conditions or the following hset/expire lines.

items.defectStatement: Making `.contents` a flex container (header.scss:17-18) makes the `header-extra-info` component's outer Ember `div.ember-view` — a direct child of `.contents` — the flex item, but that element has no class and keeps the default `min-width: auto`. The `overflow: hidden` that constrains the title lives on the inner `.extra-info-wrapper` (topic-post.scss:518) and the ellipsis on `.topic-link`, so for a non-wrapping (`white-space: nowrap`) long topic title the outer flex item cannot shrink below its min-content width, the title does not ellipsize, and the item pushes the `.panel` navigation out of the header.
obligations: The header-extra-info flex item (the component's root element that is a direct child of `.contents`) must be shrinkable below its content's intrinsic width — its used minimum width must be 0 (e.g. `min-width: 0` on that element, or an overflow value other than `visible` applied to that same element).

Long, non-wrapping topic titles must still be truncated with a CSS ellipsis inside the available width (nowrap + overflow hidden + text-overflow: ellipsis must continue to apply and actually clip the text).
The navigation `.panel` (order 3 / margin-left: auto) must remain within the header width when the title is long — the flex line must not overflow horizontally.

Existing behavior must be preserved: `align-items: center` vertical centering of the header items, the narrow-screen `.extra-info-wrapper { display: none }` media query, and the `two-rows` / second-row layout.
items.notes: The real flex item is the component's unclassed outer `div.ember-view`; `header-extra-info.hbs` nests `.extra-info-wrapper` inside it, so rules on `.extra-info-wrapper` (including the pre-existing `order: 2` and its `overflow: hidden`) do not directly govern the flex item. Two valid fixes: (a) give the component root a class and apply `min-width: 0` (and/or `overflow: hidden`) to it, or (b) set the component's tagName/classNames so the component element itself is `.extra-info-wrapper`, which puts the existing `overflow: hidden` on the flex item (a non-visible overflow makes the automatic minimum size 0). Both satisfy the obligations; a fix is not required to use a specific one. Note `order: 2` on `.extra-info-wrapper` is inert as written (not a child of `.contents`); mentioning/moving it is acceptable but out of the strictly cited defect. The finding is accurate — do not treat `align-items:center` itself as the bug.

items.defectStatement: MetricAlertDetectorHandler was changed to subclass StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate] but only declares `pass`, so it implements none of the abstract members it must provide: evaluate (inherited from DetectorHandler) plus StatefulDetectorHandler's counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. Because the class still has abstract methods, ABCMeta makes it non-instantiable, so `group_type.detector_handler(self)` in Detector.detector_handler (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86) raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class MetricAlertDetectorHandler`; previously (subclassing DetectorHandler with an evaluate override) it was instantiable, so this is a regression.
obligations: MetricAlertDetectorHandler (or whatever base it derives from) must be concrete/instantiable: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` must not raise TypeError, so `Detector.detector_handler` returns a handler rather than raising for a Detector whose type resolves to MetricAlertFire.

The four abstract StatefulDetectorHandler members (the counter_names property, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, build_occurrence_and_event_data) must be provided or otherwise satisfied by a concrete base class.

evaluate must be implemented (it is abstract too) or inherited concretely; it should remain callable and consistent with the current DetectorHandler.evaluate contract of returning a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey (the old list-returning signature is stale), and must not raise for a normal data packet.
No change to MetricAlertFire's registration/id/slug or the fact that it exposes detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler.
items.notes: The finding's list of missing methods undercounts by one: evaluate is also abstract (DetectorHandler.evaluate, detector.py:125) and was deleted in this diff, so the class is missing five abstract members, not four. The finding is otherwise accurate — MetricAlertFire is auto-registered via GroupType.__init_subclass__ (issues/grouptype.py:163-165), so the defect is reachable, not dead code. Valid fixes include: implementing all abstract methods, reverting MetricAlertDetectorHandler to a concrete/non-abstract base (with its old returning behavior) or adding the necessary overrides/delegations. The previous behavior of evaluate was to return an empty collection ([]); note the base now types it as a dict, so a fix must pick a signature consistent with the base and callers (process_detectors calls handler.evaluate(...).values()). The pre-existing TODO comment claiming this "will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction" suggests the StatefulDetectorHandler change may be premature.

items.defectStatement: In `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` (src/sentry/api/helpers/error_upsampling.py:47-65), the y-axis column is only compared against the exact literal `"count()"` after lowercasing/stripping, so valid count aggregates that differ in internal whitespace/parenthesis spacing or that carry an alias (e.g. `count() as total`, `COUNT ( )`) are passed through unchanged. Since callers pass raw request yAxis values (base `get_event_stats_data` only maps the legacy `event_count`/`user_count` aliases and otherwise forwards the string verbatim), those queries silently keep unweighted `count()` for allowlisted projects instead of `upsampled_count()`, breaking the upsampling contract.
obligations: Every y-axis entry the downstream search parser resolves to the `count()` aggregate must be transformed to the upsampled form, regardless of letter case, surrounding whitespace, and whitespace inside the parentheses (e.g. `COUNT()`, ` count() `, `count( )`).

If the count entry carries an alias, the transformation must preserve that alias (e.g. `count() as total` -> `upsampled_count() as total`); it must not force the alias to `count` or drop a non-`count` alias.
Non-count entries (other aggregations such as `count_unique(user)`, plain columns, equations) must be returned unchanged.
Existing behavior for a bare count must be preserved: `count()`, `COUNT()`, and ` count() ` still yield `upsampled_count() as count`, and the returned list stays 1:1 with the input sequence.
items.notes: The existing tests (tests/sentry/api/helpers/test_error_upsampling.py:54-75) pin the exact output `upsampled_count() as count` for unaliased count plus case/outer-whitespace insensitivity; a fix must keep those passing. The only caller is organization_events_stats.py:223 via get_event_stats_data, which forwards raw yAxis strings (get_query_columns only rewrites `event_count`/`user_count`). Valid fixes include the suggested parser-based normalization or a regex/split-on-`as` normalization, as long as alias preservation and pass-through of other columns hold. Note the finding's "parentheses variations" is real for whitespace-only differences such as `count( )`; do not over-broaden to non-count functions like `count_unique`/`count_if`. Equations are supplied through the separate `equations` parameter, so equation strings containing `count()` in the y-axis list are out of the core scope.

items.defectStatement: In testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup registrations at the cited lines use the literal alias "alias" (`testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove`, lines 381 and 425) although the IDPs are created with aliases "idp-alias-0".."idp-alias-19" and "idp-alias-20". No provider has alias "alias", so the registered cleanup never removes any of the created IDPs and test state leaks into subsequent tests. (Note: the finding's claim of an NPE is inaccurate — `get("alias")` returns a non-null JAX-RS proxy and TestCleanup.addCleanup swallows all exceptions, so the failure is silent non-cleanup, not a thrown error.)
obligations: The per-iteration cleanup inside the `for (int i = 0; i < 20; i++)` loop must remove the IDP with alias "idp-alias-" + i, so all 20 created IDPs are actually deleted after the test.
The cleanup registered after creating the extra provider (alias "idp-alias-20") must remove alias "idp-alias-20".
The cleanup must tolerate an alias whose IDP no longer exists (e.g. "idp-alias-1", which is explicitly removed at line 428) without producing a test failure or error.
The existing test logic must be preserved: IDP creation with the same aliases/config, organization linkage of idp-alias-10..19, and all in-test assertions and manual removals/updates unchanged.
items.notes: Two valid fix shapes: (a) replace get("alias") with get("idp-alias-" + i) in the loop and get("idp-alias-20") at line 425, or (b) use the idiomatic getCleanup().addIdentityProviderAlias("idp-alias-" + i) / addIdentityProviderAlias("idp-alias-20"), which internally catches NotFoundException. The eager-evaluation of `expr::method` makes `get("idp-alias-" + i)::remove` legal despite the non-final loop variable i, so no extra final-variable refactor is needed. TestCleanup.addCleanup wraps the AutoCloseable in try/catch that ignores all exceptions, so a naive fix will not break the test even if it tries to delete an already-removed IDP (e.g. idp-alias-1). The identical defect also exists in testCacheIDPByOrg at line 303 ("org-idp-" + i), but that line is outside the cited range and is not required to be fixed here.

items.defectStatement: The finding's regression claim is not substantiated by the shown code. The clause added at IdentityProviderStorageProvider.LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() (lines 253-254) is shared, but the only login-template consumer, IdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate() (services/.../IdentityProviderBean.java:226), is overridden by OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean (lines 86-97), which already applies the same/stronger organization-publicity filter (isPublicOrganizationBroker requires BROKER_PUBLIC == true). OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean is substituted for IdentityProviderBean whenever the organization feature is enabled and the realm has organizations enabled (FreeMarkerLoginFormsProvider:482-486), and the plain IdentityProviderBean is used only when organizations are disabled, where organization-linked IDPs are not meaningfully available for login. So the added clause does not change the effective federated/linked IDP list for either caller. (It is, however, required for the Infinispan login-cache invalidation that also uses getLoginPredicate.)
obligations: If the clause is moved/refactored, the Infinispan login-cache invalidation logic (registerIDPLoginInvalidation and registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate, InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider:382-418) must still classify an IDP as login-relevant when it is enabled, not link-only, not hide-on-login, and either has organizationId == null or is organization-linked with BROKER_PUBLIC == "true"; a change of BROKER_PUBLIC from false to true on an org-linked IDP must still invalidate the (realm, FetchMode) login caches.

The set of IDPs returned to the login/account-linking pages must not change: getForLogin and the IdentityProviderBean / OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean federated provider lists must keep filtering out non-public organization-linked IDPs in org-aware mode, and keep returning realm-level IDPs (organizationId == null) regardless of any BROKER_PUBLIC config.
An IDP with organizationId != null and no (or non-"true") BROKER_PUBLIC config value must be treated as not public / not login-relevant; null config values must not cause an NPE.

getLoginPredicate()/getLoginSearchOptions() must still be usable by existing callers without changing their contract (non-null input test plus enabled/link-only/hide-on-login filters), and the value returned must remain effectively immutable-safe to stream over values().
items.notes: Main trap: the finding overlooks OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.federatedProviderPredicate() (services/src/main/java/org/keycloak/organization/forms/login/freemarker/model/OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean.java:86), which is the bean actually used when organizations are enabled; its default branch already returns idp.getOrganizationId() == null || isPublicOrganizationBroker(idp), so the new clause is strictly redundant there, and in onlyRealmBrokers/onlyOrganizationBrokers modes it is also subsumed. The plain IdentityProviderBean is only instantiated when Profile.Feature.ORGANIZATION is off or the realm does not enable organizations. An alternative valid fix (and arguably cleaner design) is exactly what the finding proposes — keep the login-availability clause out of the shared SPI predicate and add a dedicated predicate (e.g. getLoginCachePredicate()) used only by InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider — but note this is a behavior-preserving refactor, not a bug fix. A fix that merely deletes the clause is NOT correct: it would break login-cache invalidation for org-linked IDPs whose BROKER_PUBLIC changes. The finding's mention of 'account-linking' is imprecise; the account console does not consume this predicate. Whether the reviewer's change is accepted as a refactor or flagged as a non-issue, the behavioral requirements above must hold.

items.defectStatement: In the "Illegal HTML" message construction (lines 102-111), the common-prefix length `start` and common-suffix length `end` are computed independently, so whenever the prefix and suffix overlap (start + end > length of `value` or of `sanitized`) the end index `length() - end` becomes smaller than `start` and `substring(start, length() - end)` throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. The exception is a RuntimeException that escapes `verifySafeHtml()`/`verify()` (only IOException is caught), aborting the theme-verifier run instead of adding the offending key's message; e.g. value="aaa" vs sanitized="aa" yields start=2,end=2 and both substring calls fail.
obligations: The message-building code must never throw (e.g. StringIndexOutOfBoundsException) for any value/sanitized pair, in particular when start + end exceeds the length of either string: bounds must be clamped so that beginIndex <= endIndex, beginIndex >= 0 and endIndex <= length.
Both the value.substring(...) and the sanitized.substring(...) calls must be made safe; the overlap can violate the bound on either string (they have different lengths).

Existing non-overlapping behavior must be preserved: when sanitized != value and prefix/suffix do not overlap, exactly one message of the form "Illegal HTML in key <key> for file <file>: '<trimmedValue>' vs '<trimmedSanitized>'" is added with the common prefix/suffix stripped, and the existing tests illegalHtmlTagEn/noHtml_de still report "Illegal HTML".
The verifier must continue processing the remaining keys/entries after building a message (no exception aborts the forEachRemaining loop), and the !Objects.equals(sanitized, value) guard must remain.
items.notes: The overlap arithmetic in the finding is correct and demonstrable: with value="aaa", sanitized="aa", start=2 and end=2, so value.substring(2,1) and sanitized.substring(2,0) both throw. Reachability in the sanitizer is narrow (needs a length change that leaves overlapping repeated chars at the ends, e.g. a one-char-shorter sanitized string), but any such input aborts verification, so the guard is warranted. Several fixes are valid (Math.min/Math.max clamp, capping end at min(len)-start, skipping the substring when bounds cross, etc.); the exact diff text shown in the overlapping case is unspecified, only that a message is still emitted for the key. Do not reject a fix merely because it changes the trimmed snippet in the degenerate overlap case.

items.defectStatement: In AnonDeviceService.tagDeviceUI (impl.go), the device cache key is written to a.localCache via SetDefault at line 87 before a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice is called at line 93. When CreateOrUpdateDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached (returned by updateDevice when rowsAffected == 0, i.e. a device over the limit), the cache entry is left in place. On the next request from the same device, tagDeviceUI's Get(key) at line 83 hits, returns nil, so TagDevice returns nil and anonymous authentication succeeds — the over-limit device is rejected only once, then admitted for the cache's 29-minute TTL. The cited lines (144-148) only propagate the error; the actual defect is the premature cache write inside tagDeviceUI (lines 83-95).
obligations: When CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, the device's cache key (Device.CacheKey(), the same key used by Get/SetDefault) must not remain present in a.localCache, so a subsequent TagDevice call for the same device re-invokes CreateOrUpdateDevice and again returns ErrDeviceLimitReached.

On a successful CreateOrUpdateDevice, existing behavior is preserved: the cache key is populated so repeated tagDeviceUI calls for the same device short-circuit (cache hit returns nil) without a DB write.

The ErrDeviceLimitReached error must still propagate from tagDeviceUI through TagDevice (the added `return err` at the cited lines) so client.go's errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) check in Authenticate still rejects the request.

A transient/non-limit CreateOrUpdateDevice failure must not leave a stale cache entry that causes the retry to be skipped (if the fix removes the entry only for ErrDeviceLimitReached, this is acceptable per current semantics since non-limit errors are only logged and auth proceeds).
items.notes: Two variants are both valid: (a) delete the key (a.localCache.Cache.Delete(key) — CacheService embeds *gocache.Cache) when CreateOrUpdateDevice fails, or (b) move SetDefault to after the successful write. The finding correctly identifies the bug; note the err variable at line 144-148 is the outer err; tagDeviceUI's internal err is shadowed inside the if at line 93. A fix restricted to the cited lines alone (only `return err`) does NOT fix the bug — the change must affect tagDeviceUI's cache ordering or add cleanup, which lives around lines 83-95. localcache.New(29*time.Minute, 15*time.Minute) sets the TTL referenced in the finding.

items.defectStatement: In `next-auth-options.ts`, the password check at line 121 runs only when `credentials.totpCode` is empty, while the new backup-code branch at line 131 runs whenever `credentials.backupCode` is truthy and `user.twoFactorEnabled` — and it never verifies the TOTP code. Consequently a request supplying any non-empty dummy `totpCode` together with a valid `backupCode` skips password verification entirely and also never verifies TOTP, allowing login with only a leaked backup code plus the victim's email. (For a normal request that sends only `backupCode`, the password is still checked, so only the combined totpCode+backupCode case is exploitable.)
obligations: A login request that supplies a valid backupCode must not authenticate unless the account password is also verified (or requests carrying both a totpCode and a backupCode must be rejected), so that a leaked backup code plus email alone cannot log in.
Legitimate backup-code login (correct password + valid backup code, no totpCode) must still succeed, and the used backup code must still be removed from the stored set.
Legitimate TOTP login (correct password + valid totpCode, no backupCode) must still succeed and be verified as before.
An invalid backup code must still fail with ErrorCode.IncorrectBackupCode and must not consume/modify any stored backup code; missing backup codes must still fail with ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes.
items.notes: Finding is accurate. Two independent valid fixes: (a) always run the password verification when a backupCode is present regardless of totpCode, or (b) reject requests that send both totpCode and backupCode (then also ensure the password check fires). The UI (apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx) clears totpCode when switching to backup-code entry, so requiring password whenever backupCode is supplied does not break the normal flow. Note the same totpCode-gated conditions exist at lines 113/117 for third-party identity providers, but the cited defect is specifically the backup-code path bypassing the password check. Trap: `credentials.backupCode` being empty string is falsy, so the branch is only entered for a non-empty code — a fix must not require the password check only when totpCode is empty.
